title: The Fabulous Discomfort of Exit Interviews
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece makes the case for exit interviews as an undervalued source of organizational feedback, noting that only about half of organizations actually conduct them because managers dread hearing criticism from disgruntled departing employees. It argues that even venting from an upset former employee usually contains useful, actionable insight worth extracting. The author provides a specific list of ten exit-interview questions and recommends the process be run by an independent third party in a short, focused conversation.
points: Only about half of organizations conduct exit interviews, largely because managers dread facing criticism from departing employees.
Even venting or complaints from disgruntled former employees usually contain useful, actionable insight.
The article offers ten specific exit-interview questions covering expectations, culture, recognition, and retention.
Ideal exit interviews are conducted in person by an independent third party and last 30 minutes or less.
Leaders must decide what feedback to act on and what to set aside as understandable but unrepresentative venting.
quotes: When they conduct Exit Interviews with team members who leave the team for whatever reason, the best organizations garner a wealth of valuable information about how to improve.
Exit Interviews and the data they provide are typically dreaded by the leaders who manage the departing colleague.
But, even in upset, the criticisms of those who leave usually contain kernels of truth that are worth acting on.
Did you feel as if your team leader invested in you and supported your success?
Exit Interviews are a best practice for an important reason. The best leaders want to know why people really left and what they can possibly do about it.
